[5 carving; 7 examples] Item 5: the carve's formula is internally inconsistent. It writes 'e[n] = q[n] - x[n] + a·(e[n-1]) for a first-order predictor a' yet concludes the error transfer function is H(z) = 1/(1-az⁻¹) — that is the transfer from the error INPUT to the error OUTPUT (a resonator that AMPLIFIES, 1/(1-az⁻¹)), not a noise-shaping feedback path, and with 0<a<1 a high-pass shape is not what 1/(1-az⁻¹) is at all (it is low-pass, peaking at DC). A first-order NTF is 1-az⁻¹ (high-pass). The definition names the wrong transfer function for the very mechanism it claims, and a formula that contradicts itself fails item 5's 'correct — formulas consistent with themselves'. Item 7 follows: the examples are anchored to that mis-stated mechanism (the 'high-pass noise shaping' in the SoX dither example is in fact SoX's TPDF/dither implementation, not a documented first-order shaping NTF). Carve is otherwise a real technique, so this is a strike on the filing's own words, not a thin-carve dispute.

payload.name: acceleration-features
payload.scope: People made acceleration features to capture the curvature, the rate of change of the velocity, of a spectral feature sequence, adding the second-order dynamics of phoneme transitions to the feature vector.

definition.body: Acceleration features (delta-delta features) are the second temporal derivative of a sequence of base acoustic features, obtained by applying the same weighted least-squares line fit to the delta sequence. For a base feature f(t) and its delta d(t), the acceleration at frame t is the delta of d computed over the same sliding window of half-width K with the same weight vector: d2(t) = argmin_d sum_{k=-K}^{K} w(k) * (d(t+k) - (a*t + b))^2. Equivalently it is the second derivative (2a) of a quadratic least-squares fit to f over the window; for K=1 the weights [1,-2,1] annihilate constants and linear trends and respond only to curvature. Parameters: (1) the base feature sequence f(t) (typically MFCC); (2) the window half-width K (commonly K=2); (3) the weight vector (normalized [-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3] over the delta sequence for K=3). Persistence: the third block of the standard 39-dimensional HMM feature vector (12 static + 12 delta + 12 acceleration) in Kaldi compute-vad-and-extract-features and HTK HCopy, and as the delta operator applied twice in librosa. e.g.: the delta-delta block of the 39-dimensional feature vector in Kaldi compute-vad-and-extract-features for triphone HMMs; the acceleration dimensions computed by applying librosa.feature.delta twice to an MFCC sequence; the 12 delta-delta dimensions of HTK HCopy's standard MFCC+delta+delta-delta feature string | not: delta-features (first-order velocity, not curvature); static MFCC (no temporal derivative); delta-cepstral-coefficients (raw cepstral first differences, not second-order) [formal: acceleratio proprietatum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: perceptual-linear-prediction
payload.scope: People made perceptual linear prediction to produce speech features that model the Bark-scale critical-band structure of human hearing and the nonlinear loudness compression before linear prediction, giving better speaker and background robustness than raw spectral methods.

definition.body: Perceptual linear prediction coefficients are a sequence of features extracted from a speech frame by applying a Bark-scale critical-band filterbank to the power spectrum, compressing the filtered energies with a power-law nonlinearity to model the equal-loudness contours of human hearing, and projecting the compressed energies onto an orthogonal basis via discrete cosine transform. Parameters: (1) the number of Bark filters (typically 13-26); (2) the power-law exponent (typically 1/3); (3) the number of DCT coefficients retained (typically 12-17). Persistence: implemented as the plp feature pipeline in the Kaldi toolkit, as the PLP analysis routine in the HTK toolkit, and as a recognized speech feature alternative to MFCC in the librosa feature extraction interface. e.g.: the plp feature pipeline in Kaldi s3 feature extraction; the PLP coefficients computed by the PLP analysis routine in HTK HCopy for triphone HMM training; the PLP feature vector produced by applying a Bark-scale filterbank with 1/3-power compression and DCT in HTK | not: bark-scale-filterbank (the linear filterbank stage alone, without the power-law compression and DCT projection); cepstral-coefficient (raw DFT-derived coefficients, without the perceptual filterbank and power-law stages) [formal: perceptiva linearis predictio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Perceptual linear prediction coefficients are a sequence of features extracted from a speech frame by applying a Bark-scale critical-band filterbank to the power spectrum, compressing the filtered energies with a power-law nonlinearity to model the equal-loudness contours of human hearing, and projecting the compressed energies onto an orthogonal basis via discrete cosine transform. Parameters: (1) the number of Bark filters (typically 13-26); (2) the power-law exponent (typically 1/3); (3) the number of DCT coefficients retained (typically 12-17). Persistence: implemented as the plp feature pipeline in the Kaldi toolkit, as the PLP analysis routine in the HTK toolkit, and as a recognized speech feature alternative to MFCC in the librosa feature extraction interface. e.g.: the plp feature pipeline in Kaldi s3 feature extraction; the PLP coefficients computed by the PLP analysis routine in HTK HCopy for triphone HMM training; the PLP feature vector produced by applying a Bark-scale filterbank with 1/3-power compression and DCT in HTK | not: bark-scale-filterbank (the linear filterbank stage alone, without the power-law compression and DCT projection); cepstral-coefficient (raw DFT-derived coefficients, without the perceptual filterbank and power-law stages) [formal: perceptiva linearis predictio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: log-mel-spectrogram
payload.scope: People made log-mel spectrograms to compress the mel-frequency spectrogram into a perceptually-shaped, energy-density representation that is compact, robust to dynamic range, and well-suited as input for neural network acoustic models.

definition.body: A log-mel spectrogram is the logarithm of the mel-frequency spectrogram, obtained by computing a short-time Fourier transform, mapping the resulting linear frequency bins onto the mel-scale via a triangular filterbank, summing the squared magnitude coefficients within each filter, and applying a base-10 or natural logarithm to compress the dynamic range. Parameters: (1) the window function and hop size (e.g., Hann window, 25ms window, 10ms hop); (2) the number of mel filters (typically 40-128); (3) the mel frequency range (e.g., 0-8000 Hz). Persistence: implemented as the librosa feature mel-spectrogram with log scaling (librosa.feature.melspectrogram + np.log), in the Kaldi featbin compute-fbank feature extraction with log option, and as the torchaudio transforms Melspectrogram + LogOperation in PyTorch audio pipelines. e.g.: librosa feature.melspectrogram with log1p for Kaldi Librispeech ASR; Kaldi compute-fbank with --log-fbank=true for NN acoustic training; torchaudio.transforms.Melspectrogram with log1p in speech recognition training | not: mel-frequency-cepstrum (cepstral coefficients derived from log-mel via DCT, not the log-mel representation itself); mel-filterbank (the linear filterbank before log compression) [formal: logarithmica mel spectographema | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstrum-time-warping
payload.scope: People made cepstral time warping to non-uniformly modify the quefrency axis of a cepstrum, compressing formant-dense regions to improve alignment and speaker robustness.

definition.body: Cepstral time warping is a technique that modifies the quefrency axis of a cepstrum by non-uniform warping to align the temporal structure of speech frames, compressing or expanding low-quefrency regions where formant-related information concentrates while preserving high-quefrency voicing periodicity. The procedure: apply a nonlinear mapping function q' = f(q) to each quefrency value q, where f is typically a logarithmic or power-law function that compresses low quefrencies. The warped cepstrum is then transformed back to the time or frequency domain via inverse transform. Parameters: (1) the warping function (logarithmic, power-law, or custom); (2) the warping parameter controlling compression strength; (3) the quefrency range to warp. Persistence: implemented in cepstral analysis software for speaker normalization and in robust speech recognition front-ends as a preprocessing step before feature extraction. e.g.: cepstral quefrency warping applied for speaker normalization in Kaldi's i-vector extraction pipeline; logarithmic quefrency warping in HTK cepstral analysis for improved formant alignment; custom quefrency warping in the VoiceCept speaker recognition toolkit | not: cepstral-subband (dividing the cepstral domain into frequency bands without non-uniform warping); cepstral-smoothing (low-pass filtering of cepstral coefficients, not quefrency-axis warping) [formal: quefrequenti temporis deformatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: log-frequency-spectrum
payload.scope: People made log-frequency spectra to represent spectral energy uniformly spaced in pitch space, so that equal channel intervals correspond to equal perceptual frequency ratios rather than equal absolute differences.

definition.body: A log-frequency spectrum represents the power spectral density of a signal using filterbank channels spaced uniformly on a logarithmic frequency axis, typically one or more channels per musical octave, so that equal channel spacing corresponds to equal perceptual pitch intervals. Procedure: compute the short-time Fourier transform of the signal, map the linear frequency bins to a logarithmic scale via a bank of overlapping triangular or Gaussian filters with geometrically spaced center frequencies f_k = f_0 * 2^(k/n) where n is channels per octave, and sum the spectral energy within each filter passband. Parameters: (1) the sampling rate and FFT size; (2) channels per octave (commonly 12 for semitone resolution); (3) the reference frequency and frequency range; (4) the filter shape (triangular, Gaussian, or constant-Q derived). Persistence: implemented in MIRtoolbox and libmirt for music information retrieval, in the Aubio logfilterbank for audio analysis, and in the librosa feature logspec for acoustic modeling. e.g.: 12-channels-per-octave log-frequency spectrum in MIRtoolbox logspec() for chord recognition; Aubio logfilterbank with 24 channels per octave for pitch extraction; librosa.feature.logspec with default 12-chorus resolution for timbre classification; Google Magenta's log-frequency spectrogram for music transcription | not: mel-spectrum (uses psychoacoustic mel-scale with unequal perceptual spacing per bin); log-mel-spectrogram (logarithm of mel-energy, not log-spaced filterbank itself) [formal: spectrum logarithmicae frequentiae | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: feature-pyramid
payload.scope: People made feature pyramids to organize signal representations across multiple resolution scales, enabling multi-scale analysis of music and speech structures from fine temporal detail to broad temporal envelopes.

definition.body: A feature pyramid is a multi-resolution representation that organizes acoustic or spectral features into layers of decreasing temporal resolution and increasing contextual span, where each layer is derived from the previous by a downsampling operation (averaging, max-pooling, or stride). Procedure: begin with a base feature sequence (e.g., mel-frequency spectrogram or log-frequency spectrum at frame rate 100+ Hz), then iteratively apply a pooling or averaging operation with a fixed stride factor (typically 2x) to produce successively coarser layers. Parameters: (1) the base feature and its frame rate; (2) the downsampling stride per level; (3) the number of pyramid levels; (4) the pooling function (average, max, or learned). Persistence: used as input representation in deep neural network acoustic models including Wav2Vec 2.0 feature pyramids, in the Kaldi multi-scale xvector extraction pipeline, and in PyTorch Audio's feature-pyramid modules for music and speech tasks. e.g.: Wav2Vec 2.0 multi-layer feature pyramid for self-supervised speech representation learning; Kaldi multi-scale xvector extraction with averaged pooling across frame-rate layers; PyTorch Audio FeaturePyramid for hierarchical timbre modeling; Google's multi-resolution spectrogram pyramid for source separation [formal: pyramis characteristcum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-pitch
payload.scope: People made cepstral pitch to estimate pitch period directly from the quefrency domain of a cepstrum, where the dominant quefrency peak corresponds to the glottal cycle period of voiced speech.

definition.body: Cepstral pitch is a pitch estimation method that extracts the fundamental period from the quefrency domain representation of a signal, where the strongest low-quefrency peak corresponds to the pitch period of voiced speech. Procedure: compute the cepstrum of a speech frame via FFT of the log magnitude spectrum (or LPC cepstrum), locate the peak in the quefrency range corresponding to plausible pitch periods (typically 2–20 ms for adult speech, mapping to 50–500 Hz), and convert the quefrency of that peak to frequency via f = sampling_rate / quefrency_sample. Parameters: (1) the cepstrum type (FFT cepstrum, LPC cepstrum, or complex cepstrum); (2) the quefrency search range bounded by minimum and maximum pitch period; (3) the peak detection threshold and validation via quefrency-domain SNR. Persistence: implemented as the cepstral pitch detection algorithm in speech analysis toolkits, taught in speech processing curricula alongside autocorrelation and YIN methods, and used in prosody analysis and voice conversion pipelines. e.g.: cepstral pitch estimation in HTK HPSS module for prosody analysis; Kaldi's cepstral pitch extractor using the LPC cepstrum peak in the plausible F0 range; Praat's cepstral pitch analysis option for voice quality assessment; Speech Toolbox cepstral pitch tracking in MATLAB audio analysis [formal: pitch quefrequenti | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: harmonic-product-spectrum
payload.scope: People made the harmonic product spectrum to estimate fundamental frequency from the harmonic structure of a signal's spectrum by multiplying spectrally-downsampled copies, amplifying the periodicity where harmonics align.

definition.body: The harmonic product spectrum is a pitch estimation technique that multiplies the downsampled power spectrum of a signal across multiple octave-shifted copies, so that the fundamental frequency peak is amplified where harmonics at integer multiples align. Procedure: (1) compute the magnitude spectrum |X(k)| of a signal frame; (2) downsample by integer factors m=2,3,...,M by taking every m-th sample; (3) multiply the original and downsampled spectra pointwise: H(k) = |X(k)| * |X(2k)| * |X(3k)| * ... * |X(Mk)|; (4) locate the peak in H(k) within a plausible fundamental frequency range. The multiplication amplifies peaks at the true fundamental while suppressing inharmonic noise. Parameters: (1) the FFT size and window function; (2) the downsampling depth M (typically 3–8); (3) the search range for the fundamental peak. Persistence: implemented in the librosa harmonic_pitch_feature pipeline, in theaubio harmonic product spectrum module, and as a standard pitch estimation baseline in computational musicology and speech analysis toolkits. e.g.: librosa.feature.harmonic_pitch_feature with default downsampling factors for pitch contour extraction; aubio hpss harmonic product spectrum module for fundamental frequency estimation; MATLAB Signal Processing Toolbox pitch estimator using harmonic product for musical instrument analysis; Praat harmonic product analysis for voice fundamental tracking [formal: spectrum harmonicum productum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-delay
payload.scope: People made cepstral delay to represent the quefrency-domain equivalent of time delay, measuring the temporal offset between two signals in the cepstral domain as a robust alternative to cross-correlation for speech and audio alignment.

definition.body: Cepstral delay is a measure of the time offset between two signals computed in the quefrency domain of their cepstrum, where the quefrency of the peak in the cross-cepstrum corresponds to the delay between the signals. Procedure: (1) compute the FFT of both signals; (2) compute the complex cepstrum of each; (3) compute the cross-cepstrum via inverse FFT of the product of one spectrum's complex conjugate and the other's; (4) locate the peak quefrency in the cross-cepstrum, which corresponds to the delay. The peak in the cross-cepstrum occurs at the quefrency equal to the inter-signal delay, making it analogous to cross-correlation but with better noise robustness for tonal signals. Parameters: (1) the FFT size and window function; (2) the quefrency search range constrained by maximum expected delay; (3) the cepstrum type (complex, LP, or standard). Persistence: used in speech alignment and speaker diarization pipelines in the HTK toolkit, in the Kaldi voice conversion delay estimation module, and in the speech toolbox for robust time-delay estimation in reverberant conditions. e.g.: Kaldi's cepstral-delay estimation for voice conversion alignment in the vocoder pipeline; HTK cepstral cross-correlation for speaker diarization in the SPHERE evaluation toolkit; Speech Toolbox cepstral delay estimation for robust alignment in noisy conditions; Praat cepstral cross-cepstrum analysis for speech synchronization [formal: quefrequenti mora | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-lag

definition.body: The cepstral cross-cepstrum is a function on the quefrency axis that measures the similarity between two signals as a time-shift function, computed by taking the inverse Fourier transform of the product of one signal's magnitude spectrum and the complex conjugate of the other's spectrum. Procedure: (1) compute the DFT of both signals X(f) and Y(f); (2) compute the cross-spectrum S(f) = |X(f)| * conj(Y(f)); (3) take the natural logarithm ln(S(f)); (4) apply the inverse DFT to obtain the cross-cepstrum C(q). The peak in C(q) at non-zero quefrency q₀ gives the time delay between the signals. Parameters: (1) the FFT size and window function; (2) the quefrency search range; (3) whether to use real or complex cepstrum. payload.name: cepstral-centroid
payload.scope: People made cepstral-centroid to quantify the spectral balance point of a speech signal in the quefrency domain, identifying whether energy concentrates in low-quefrency (vocal-tract) or high-quefrency (pitch-related) components.

definition.body: The cepstral-centroid is a scalar feature that computes the center-of-mass of a signal's cepstrum across quefrency, yielding a single value that indicates whether spectral energy concentrates in low-quefrency (formant/shape) or high-quefrency (periodicity/pitch) regions. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of the input signal via FFT, log-power spectrum, and inverse FFT; (2) optionally apply a real-valued weighting function w[q] over quefrency (commonly w[q]=1 or a window that suppresses very-high-quefrency noise); (3) compute the weighted sum of quefrency values multiplied by cepstral magnitudes, divided by the sum of the weights: centroid = Σ(q · w[q] · |c[q]|) / Σ(w[q] · |c[q]|). Parameters: (1) the input signal or its cepstrum coefficients, (2) the quefrency range over which to compute the statistic, (3) the optional weighting function. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech analysis toolkits (Praat, librosa), used in speech quality assessment, prosody analysis, and voice disorder detection, documented in speech processing literature. e.g.: Praat's cepstral centroid computation for voice quality analysis; librosa's cepstral centroid for timbre characterization in audio analysis; Rabiner and Schafer's cepstral statistics for speaker characterization | not: spectral-centroid (frequency-domain analogue, not quefrency-based); cepstral-envelope (the full spectral envelope shape, not a single scalar statistic) [formal: centrum cepstrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-peak
payload.scope: People made cepstral-peak to isolate individual maxima in a cepstrum that correspond to distinct periodicities or echo delays in a signal.

definition.body: A cepstral-peak is a single local maximum in the cepstrum at a specific quefrency value q₀, representing a dominant periodicity in the signal (low quefrency → vocal tract formants; high quefrency → pitch period). A cepstrum may contain multiple peaks, each corresponding to a distinct delay or periodicity. The procedure to identify a cepstral-peak: (1) compute the cepstrum c[q] of the signal; (2) scan the quefrency axis for local maxima where c[q₀] > c[q] for all q in some neighborhood (q₀-Δ, q₀+Δ); (3) record the quefrency location q₀ and magnitude c[q₀]. Parameters: (1) the cepstrum signal or its quefrency-domain representation, (2) the quefrency search range (e.g., 1 ms–20 ms for speech pitch), (3) the neighborhood radius Δ for local comparison. Persistence mechanism: implemented in pitch detection algorithms (e.g., RAPT, PYPE), echo detection systems, and speech analysis toolkits; documented in signal processing literature. e.g.: RAPT algorithm's cepstral peak detection for pitch period estimation in speech analysis; HTK's cepstrum-based echo detection using peak quefrency location; Praat's cepstral peak picking for voice fundamental frequency estimation | not: cepstral-peak-picking (the algorithm to find peaks, not the peak itself); cepstral-distance (a measure between two cepstra, not a single peak) [formal: cacumen cepstrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pitch-period
payload.scope: People made pitch-period to specify the time interval between consecutive glottal closures in voiced speech, serving as the fundamental timescale for voicing analysis and pitch estimation.

definition.body: The pitch-period (often denoted T₀) is the time duration between successive periodic pulses in a voiced speech signal, corresponding to the fundamental frequency F₀ = 1/T₀. It represents the time interval between consecutive vocal fold closures during phonation. The procedure to estimate pitch-period from a speech signal: (1) compute a periodicity measure — either via cepstral peak location in the quefrency domain, autocorrelogram peak, or time-domain zero-crossing; (2) identify the dominant peak in the periodicity function within the search range (typically 1.5–12 ms for adult speech); (3) the lag at this peak is the estimated pitch-period T₀. Parameters: (1) the speech signal frame or its derived representation, (2) the quefrency/lag search range (e.g., 1.5 ms–12 ms), (3) the minimum pitch expected (e.g., 60 Hz for adult males). Persistence mechanism: implemented in pitch estimation algorithms (RAPT, YIN, SWIPE, PYPE), speech synthesis systems (STRAIGHT, WORLD), and analysis toolkits (Praat, librosa); documented in speech processing literature. e.g.: RAPT algorithm's cepstral pitch-period estimation for speaker normalization; YIN algorithm's autocorrelation-based pitch-period detection in audio analysis; Praat's pitch-period measurement for fundamental frequency contour extraction | not: fundamental-frequency (the rate F₀ in Hz, not the time interval T₀); glottal-flow (the airflow waveform through the glottis, not its periodicity) [formal: periodus fundamentalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-coding
payload.scope: People made cepstral-coding to compactly represent speech cepstral coefficients for storage and transmission in speech coding and recognition systems.

definition.body: Cepstral-coding is the set of techniques for quantizing, compressing, and encoding cepstral coefficients into a compact bit-stream representation suitable for storage or transmission. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstral coefficients (e.g., MFCCs or LPCCs) of a speech frame; (2) apply differential encoding (e.g., DPCM — differential pulse code modulation) between consecutive frames to exploit temporal redundancy; (3) quantize the differential values to a fixed number of bits using scalar or vector quantization; (4) encode the quantized values using entropy coding (e.g., Huffman coding) or packetize for network transmission. Parameters: (1) the number of cepstral coefficients to encode (e.g., 12–13 for MFCCs), (2) the quantization bit-depth (e.g., 8–16 bits per coefficient), (3) the frame rate (e.g., 10 ms frames). Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech coding standards (e.g., G.711/MCELP, G.729/CS-ACELP, AMR), speech recognition systems, and telecommunication protocols; documented in ITU-T standards and speech coding literature. e.g.: ITU-T G.729's CS-ACELP codec using differential encoding of cepstral parameters; AMR-NB codec's frame-by-frame quantization of speech cepstral features for cellular transmission; CELP-based speech coders in VoIP systems using 4-bit differential cepstral quantization | not: cepstral-compression (lossless compression of stored cepstra, not coding for transmission); cepstral-quantization (the quantization step alone, not the full coding pipeline) [formal: codificatio cepstralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pitch-saliency
payload.scope: People made pitch-saliency to measure the perceptual strength or prominence of pitch in a speech or audio signal, distinguishing voiced from unvoiced segments.

definition.body: Pitch-saliency is a scalar measure that quantifies how strongly a pitch (fundamental frequency) is perceived in a speech or audio signal at a given time frame. Higher saliency indicates a clear, easily detectable pitch (voiced speech); lower saliency indicates weak or absent pitch (unvoiced speech, noise). The procedure to compute pitch-saliency: (1) compute a periodicity function — either the autocorrelogram R[τ] or the cepstrum c[q] over a pitch-relevant lag range; (2) normalize the function, e.g., R[0] = 1 for autocorrelogram; (3) extract the saliency as the ratio of the peak value (at the dominant pitch lag) to the average or baseline of the function: saliency = R[τ_peak] / mean(R[τ]). Parameters: (1) the input signal frame or its periodicity representation, (2) the pitch search range (e.g., 50–500 Hz), (3) the normalization method. Persistence mechanism: implemented in voice activity detection (VAD) systems, pitch tracking algorithms (YIN, SWIPE), and speech segmentation toolkits; documented in speech processing and auditory modeling literature. e.g.: YIN algorithm's pitch-saliency measure (difference function ratio) for voiced/unvoiced decision in audio analysis; SWIPE algorithm's saliency-weighted pitch estimation for robust voice detection; Praat's pitch-saliency thresholding for voice quality assessment in phonetic analysis | not: pitch-confidence (a system-level estimate of tracking reliability, not frame-level perceptual strength); pitch-strength (the perceptual attribute itself, not the computational measure) [formal: eminentia fundamentalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-whitening
payload.scope: People made cepstral-whitening to flatten the cepstral representation, removing the spectral envelope's influence and leaving only fine spectral structure for speaker-independent recognition.

definition.body: Cepstral-whitening is a signal processing procedure that flattens the spectral envelope of a signal by equalizing the cepstrum, preserving only the fine spectral structure (residual) while suppressing the slowly-varying formant envelope. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of the input signal via FFT, log-power spectrum, and inverse FFT; (2) design a cepstral low-pass filter (the lifter) to isolate the spectral envelope component in the quefrency domain; (3) subtract the envelope cepstrum from the original cepstrum, yielding the residual (whitened) cepstrum; (4) optionally inverse-transform the residual back to the frequency domain. Parameters: (1) the input signal or its cepstrum, (2) the cepstral lifter order (quefrency cutoff separating envelope from residual), (3) whether the output is kept in cepstral or frequency domain. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speaker recognition front-ends (e.g., CMVN variants, PLP), speech enhancement systems, and acoustic modeling pipelines; documented in speech and speaker processing literature. e.g.: CMVN-based cepstral normalization in Kaldi's x-vector speaker recognition pipeline; PLP hearing-based processing with cepstral liftering in HTK speaker modeling; CMVN with cepstral whitening in NIST SRE speaker recognition evaluations | not: cepstral-smoothing (low-pass filtering that preserves envelope shape, not removal); cepstral-subtraction (noise removal in the cepstral domain, not envelope equalization) [formal: albalio cepstrali | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-window
payload.scope: People made cepstral-window to isolate specific quefrency bands of interest in cepstrum analysis, enabling targeted feature extraction for pitch, formant, or noise components.

definition.body: A cepstral-window is a quefrency-domain weighting function applied to a cepstrum to selectively retain or suppress specific quefrency ranges, effectively isolating components of interest (e.g., low-quefrency formants or high-quefrency pitch harmonics). The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum c[q] of the input signal; (2) define a window function W[q] that is non-zero over the desired quefrency band (e.g., a rectangular window [q_min, q_max], a raised-cosine window for smooth roll-off, or a Gaussian window centered on a target quefrency); (3) multiply the cepstrum by the window: c_w[q] = c[q] · W[q]; (4) optionally apply the inverse FFT to recover a time-domain or frequency-domain signal modified by the quefrency selection. Parameters: (1) the input cepstrum, (2) the quefrency band [q_min, q_max], (3) the window shape (rectangular, Hamming, Gaussian, etc.), (4) whether output remains in cepstral or is inverse-transformed. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech analysis toolkits (Praat, HTK, librosa), used for pitch tracking, formant analysis, and noise-cepstrum suppression; documented in speech processing literature. e.g.: Praat's cepstral windowing for isolating pitch-relevant quefrency bands in fundamental frequency estimation; HTK's cepstral windowing for formant extraction in speech analysis; librosa's quefrency-domain windowing for echo detection in audio processing | not: cepstral-lifter (a fixed low-pass or high-pass filter, not a general band-selective window); cepstral-smoothing (a low-pass operation that preserves envelope shape across the full quefrency axis) [formal: fenestra cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-homomorphic-filtering
payload.scope: People made cepstral-homomorphic-filtering to separate convolved signal components (source and filter) by transforming the signal into the cepstral domain, applying a filter, and transforming back, thereby isolating periodic structures that correspond to different physical sources.

definition.body: Cepstral-homomorphic-filtering is a signal processing method that separates convolved signals by operating in the cepstral (quefrency) domain. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of the input signal via FFT, log-power spectrum, and inverse FFT; (2) apply a quefrency-domain window (low-pass for spectral envelope extraction, high-pass for pitch detection, band-pass for component isolation); (3) inverse-transform the windowed cepstrum back to the time or frequency domain. Parameters: (1) the cepstrum type (standard, complex, or LP cepstrum), (2) the quefrency cutoff range defining the window, (3) the window shape (rectangular, Gaussian, or raised cosine). Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech processing toolkits (HTK cepstral homomorphic filtering, Kaldi's source-filter separation pipelines), audio analysis libraries (librosa's homomorphic processing utilities), and acoustic modeling systems for speaker normalization and voice conversion. e.g.: HTK cepstral homomorphic filtering for speech enhancement; Kaldi's source-filter separation in speaker recognition front-ends; librosa's homomorphic filtering for audio source separation | not: cepstral-whitening (removes the spectral envelope entirely rather than separating convolved components); cepstral-smoothing (applies smoothing to cepstral coefficients without inverse-transforming back) [formal: filtrum homomorphum cepstrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-deconvolution
payload.scope: People made cepstral-deconvolution to recover individual convolved signal components by operating in the quefrency domain, where convolution in the original domain becomes addition, enabling separation of overlapping sources.

definition.body: Cepstral-deconvolution is a signal processing technique that recovers individual components of a convolved signal by exploiting the property that convolution in the time domain corresponds to addition in the cepstral domain. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum of the observed signal via FFT, log-power spectrum, and inverse FFT; (2) apply a quefrency-domain window to isolate the component of interest (low quefrency for the slowly-varying spectral envelope, high quefrency for periodic structures); (3) inverse-transform the windowed cepstrum back to the frequency or time domain, then exponentiate to recover the separated component. Parameters: (1) the cepstrum type (standard or complex), (2) the quefrency range defining the window, (3) the window shape (rectangular, Gaussian, or raised cosine). Persistence mechanism: implemented in spectroscopy software for rolling-center removal, seismic data processing for source waveform extraction, and speech processing toolkits for source-filter separation. e.g.: rolling-center removal in X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy using cepstral deconvolution; source waveform extraction in seismic processing via cepstral windowing; vocal tract impulse response extraction from speech signals using cepstral high-pass filtering | not: cepstral-subtraction (removes additive noise in the cepstral domain rather than separating convolved components); cepstral-whitening (removes the spectral envelope entirely rather than deconvolving specific components) [formal: deconvolutio cepstrali | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]
